situation:
You are the product development manager for BOROUGH BAGEL & BAKE CO., a profitable quick-serve bagel and bakery chain with eleven shops. The founder (judge), who opened the first shop close to fifteen years ago, is preparing to sell the company and step away within the year.

Every shop still rolls and shapes its dough by hand each morning and boils it in a kettle before baking. The signs above the counters say so, and regular customers repeat the claim back to the crew. That promise, more than price, is why many of them drive past two competitors to reach a BOROUGH counter.

The founder (judge) wants a stuffed bagel sandwich on the menu before the sale closes, believing a signature item raises what a buyer will pay. Its prep is heavy. Filling, sealing and finishing each order adds close to forty minutes to a morning the crew already fills with hand-rolling, and no shop has the counter space to do both.

Buying par-baked dough from a central bakery would clear the morning for the sandwich, but it ends the hand-rolling the shops are known for and cuts crew hours in every store. Counsel says the small-batch wording on the signs could lawfully stay, though regular customers who watch the ovens would object to a claim that no longer describes the morning.

Keeping the hand-rolling and launching a simpler item instead protects the promise but leaves the founder (judge) selling a chain with no new signature product. The founder (judge) has asked you to weigh both routes and recommend one, explaining what the choice does to the brand and to the crew. The founder (judge) will greet you, hear your ideas and ask questions, then thank you for your work.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the founder (judge) of BOROUGH BAGEL & BAKE CO. Business background is the same as the situation above. You built the chain on dough rolled by hand every morning, you have told buyers the stuffed bagel sandwich will be on the menu before the sale closes, and you know the crew cannot do both jobs in the same morning.

You want the product development manager to recommend either the par-baked dough from a central bakery or a simpler new item that leaves the hand-rolling alone, and to say plainly what the recommendation does to the brand, to the crew and to the regular customers who read the signs above the counters.

During the presentation you are to ask the following questions of each participant:
judgeQuestions: Who ends up paying for the route you recommend?
Is that a fair way to spread the cost?
